question: The father is the one being held hostage, not his daughter. Over the phone, his daughter begs the kidnapper to spare his life, while the captor shouts a demand aimed at her: bring one hundred million yen alone by noon tomorrow, or the hostage dies. The father realizes the kidnapper fully intends to kill him once the money is delivered—the ransom will not save him. Worse, if his daughter brings the money alone, she will be walking straight into danger from a captor willing to harm the family. So the father decides the ransom should not be paid: paying would not save his life and would put his daughter at risk, and refusing is his way of keeping her away from the kidnapper even at the cost of his own life.

question: The father is the hostage, not the daughter. On the phone, his daughter begs the captor to spare his life, while the "kidnapper" shouts a demand aimed at her: bring one hundred million yen alone by noon tomorrow, or the hostage dies, with no police. The father therefore knows the captor is not a normal ransom-taker who will release him after payment; paying would not reliably save him, and it would send his daughter alone into the hands of someone willing to harm the family. His decision that the ransom should not be paid is thus a protective message to her: do not deliver the money, do not come alone, and do not let the kidnapper use her to reach the family—even if his own life is the price. The essential story is that a captive father, hearing the demand made to his daughter, chooses refusal to keep her out of the trap and to deny the captor his leverage.
